title: Issue 1 Cover — The Impossible Flaw
summary: Founding Shattering cover. Sell Issue 1 through one irresistible contradiction: the High Era corridor civilization is beautiful, synchronized, prosperous, and visibly trustworthy, yet one vessel exists twice along the same route. Wonder must arrive before unease. Liora notices the impossible flaw; the cover does not announce catastrophe.
panelPlan: SINGLE FULL-BLEED PORTRAIT COVER. Compose vertically with approximately the upper 55–60% devoted to the immense working corridor network, the lower 25–30% to Liora and the observation architecture, and the remaining space protected for clean integrated masthead readability.
CAMERA: slightly behind and to one side of Liora at human eye/shoulder height, not a heroic low angle. The reader should share her act of noticing rather than look up at her as an icon.

PRIMARY IMAGE: a magnificent verified-green public corridor arcs through the field with ordinary civilian/freight traffic flowing in precise, disciplined spacing. The world must look enviably functional before anything looks wrong.

THE IMPOSSIBLE FLAW: one specific vessel appears twice along the same corridor path — same hull, same orientation, same identifying silhouette — offset just enough in distance/time to be unmistakably impossible. Do not render it as a translucent ghost or digital glitch; both appearances should look physically credible.

Focal hierarchy must be: 1) the doubled vessel contradiction, 2) Liora's eyeline/reaction, 3) the grandeur of the corridor system, 4) institutional detail. The cover fails if Liora becomes the dominant poster portrait or if the anomaly is lost in background traffic.

Liora occupies roughly 12–18% of the image height. She is an adult working physicist in practical High Era engineering/research clothing, not a uniformed military officer. Her body language is still, attentive, and intellectually alarmed — no shouting, pointing, or melodramatic recoil.
Use long clean corridor arcs, stable repeated spacing, and precise civic geometry to establish visual order. The doubled vessel should be the only thing violating that grammar.
PALETTE: verified route green + luminous white/gold civic neutrals + restrained cool technical shadows. No emergency red. No dirty dystopian grading. No generic blue-neon cyberpunk wash.
LIGHTING: broad confident civic illumination with crisp subject/background separation. The corridor glow should feel infrastructural, not magical.

MASTHEAD ZONE: keep the upper 20–25% visually calm enough for a premium title block. Corridor lines may pass behind the masthead only as broad simple geometry; no ship, face, or anomaly may compete with the lettering.
THUMBNAIL READ: first, 'beautiful functioning space-road'; second, 'wait, that is the same ship twice.' The second realization is the commercial hook.
SPOILER CEILING: no corridor tearing, no collapsing beacons, no damping chamber, no red unsafe corridors, no post-Break ruins, no rescue vessel, no mature Rex Fleet ship/uniform/iconography.

MUST AVOID: generic fleet traffic poster, battle energy, obvious glitch overlays, giant warning UI, dozens of equally important ships, Liora posed as an action hero, or an anomaly so subtle it disappears when reduced.

title: Issue 2 Cover — Inherited Machinery
summary: Sell Issue 2 as inherited dependence: the High Era confidently occupies the polished upper layers of a civilization whose essential corridor machinery descends far below into systems older, heavier, and less understood than the people using them. The cover promises that an answer may exist underneath them without revealing the damping solution.
panelPlan: SINGLE FULL-BLEED PORTRAIT COVER built as one continuous architectural descent, not a split-screen. The composition should visually move from polished High Era certainty at the top into forgotten engineered depth below.

CAMERA: high oblique sectional perspective, as if the reader can see through stacked architecture. Keep believable physical continuity between inhabited upper levels, service shafts, archive access, and the older machinery below.
UPPER 30–35%: functioning High Era civic/network space with one verified-green corridor line crossing or visible beyond it. The system above still looks prosperous and dependable.

LOWER 50–55%: enormous older harmonic machinery — circular absorption forms, massive structural rings, conduits, maintenance voids, old service architecture — engineered rather than mystical. It should feel too large to have been forgotten and too embedded to be optional.

Heska is the nearest human focal figure; Liora is secondary. Keep both small against the architecture, together occupying no more than roughly 15% of frame height. Their scale is part of the selling idea.
Heska may carry or stand beside a Dawn Era schematic/provenance surface, but any marks must remain abstract and non-legible. Do not let a readable diagram explain the damping system.

One green corridor line in the upper world should bow very slightly away from its expected geometry. This is the visual tether between the civilization above and the buried system below; it must be visible but not yet catastrophic.

SHAPE LANGUAGE: upper world = planar, clean, rectilinear, repeatable; buried system = massive circular/harmonic forms, deep vertical shafts, heavy structure. The contrast should imply generational forgetting without using 'ancient temple' tropes.

PALETTE: retain white/gold/green High Era confidence above; transition downward into desaturated metals, deep neutral shadows, old ceramic/engineered surfaces, and sparse dormant green residual light. No magical blue relic glow.
LIGHTING: bright even civic light above, practical service illumination through the middle, controlled darkness below that still preserves readable engineered form.
MASTHEAD ZONE: title occupies clean upper architecture/sky. Do not place the deepest machinery behind the masthead; the cover should feel like the reader descends after reading the title.
THUMBNAIL READ: clean civilization on top / impossible depth of machinery beneath / tiny people between them.
SPOILER CEILING: do not clearly reveal the damping chamber as the solved answer, show the damping cycle, show successful access, or depict the network already collapsing.
MUST AVOID: archaeology fantasy, temple imagery, glowing prophecy symbols, steampunk decay, literal labeled cutaway graphics, or a simple 50/50 'before/after' split.

title: Issue 3 Cover — Two Instructions
summary: Sell Issue 3 through procedural collision made physical: one ancient damping apparatus is receiving two incompatible definitions of 'stable.' Liora and Alan are operating a coherent local calibration while a second clean official command path enters the same machine. The cover stops before failure.
panelPlan: SINGLE FULL-BLEED PORTRAIT COVER dominated by one large circular/elliptical damping apparatus that occupies roughly 60–70% of the frame and provides the image's strongest silhouette.

CAMERA: medium-wide inside the chamber from slightly above control-deck height, allowing the reader to see Liora/Alan, the local control path, the remote command intrusion, and the same apparatus simultaneously.

Liora is the primary human focal figure at the local control point; Alan is close beside/behind her as collaborator. They should read as a working pair inside one problem, not two separate hero portraits.

LOCAL CONTROL LANGUAGE: a coherent restrained green/white calibration geometry should visibly connect Liora's controls into the apparatus. Keep it simple enough to read as one organized instruction path.

REMOTE CONTROL LANGUAGE: a second clean official path enters from another architectural/system direction — precise, authoritative, and initially reasonable rather than visually 'evil.' Use a distinct but restrained signal treatment so the reader can see two commands reaching the same system.

The two instruction paths should remain individually orderly and only become visibly incompatible at the exact point where they converge on the apparatus. That collision point is the second focal anchor after Liora.

Do not show sparks, structural rupture, a thrown Alan, red emergency alarms, or a broken machine. The commercial tension is that the reader can see the contradiction before the characters can see its full consequence.
SHAPE LANGUAGE: one dominant harmonic circle crossed by two directional vectors. The visual sentence must be legible even if all interface detail is blurred away.
PALETTE: High Era white/gold/green baseline with one restrained contrasting official-command accent. Avoid rainbow interface color and neon technical clutter.
LIGHTING: low ambient chamber light with controlled emitter illumination tracing engineered surfaces. Faces and hands remain readable; do not silhouette the operators into anonymity.
MASTHEAD ZONE: use the upper arc of the apparatus as framing architecture but preserve a clean center/top title field. No control stream should cut through the masthead.
THUMBNAIL READ: one machine / two instructions / two engineers caught between them.
SPOILER CEILING: no failed damping cycle, no Alan injury, no manual abort, no ship echo, no propagated corridor folding, no transition to triage.

MUST AVOID: villain-face overlays, hacker imagery, beam battle, floating text walls, explosive climax imagery, or making the remote instruction visually malicious before the story earns that judgment.

title: Issue 4 Cover — The Road Breaks
summary: The season's spectacular cover. Sell a physically impossible infrastructure failure, not a battle: a High Era vessel remains intact while its verified green corridor slips out of registration and the same ship appears displaced beside itself. The road through impossible space has stopped agreeing where the traveler is.
settingText: Open High Era public corridor space near a major convergence route during the first plainly visible harmonic folding. Sparse deep space surrounds engineered green route geometry, anchor structures, and one civilian/convoy vessel. No combatants.
panelPlan: SINGLE FULL-BLEED PORTRAIT COSMIC COVER. One vessel and its displaced echo are the dominant readable forms. Keep the scene sparse enough that the geometric impossibility is instantly legible.
CAMERA: three-quarter exterior view slightly above/behind the vessel so the hull silhouette is distinctive and the corridor can be seen continuing through depth. Avoid side-profile poster flatness.
PRIMARY VESSEL: intact High Era civilian/convoy craft, not a warship, occupying roughly 30–40% of frame width. It should look designed for dependable corridor travel, not combat.

ECHO: repeat the exact same hull silhouette in a displaced position offset along a physically impossible vector — close enough that the eye instantly identifies duplication, far enough that the two silhouettes do not merge. The echo is not transparent and not a hologram.

CORRIDOR FAILURE: the verified green route bends, splits and slips out of registration around the vessel. Use offset route ribbons, mismatched anchor geometry and broken spatial alignment. The corridor itself is the disaster architecture.
Do not use explosions as the primary signal of danger. Hulls may be under stress, but the terrifying image is that the infrastructure defining safe space has become contradictory.
SHAPE LANGUAGE: stable ship silhouette duplicated against diverging green corridor vectors. Surrounding negative space should increase the wrongness.

PALETTE: deep black/blue-neutral space + vivid verified green route geometry + restrained ship neutrals. A small amount of unsafe red may appear only if logically tied to failing beacon/route verification, never as an overall disaster wash.
LIGHTING: corridor glow should rake across both hull instances consistently enough to make the duplication feel physically real. Avoid psychedelic anomaly lighting.
MASTHEAD ZONE: preserve a calmer upper region of space/corridor glow. Spectacle may frame the title but must not render it noisy.
THUMBNAIL READ: one ship, then unmistakably the same ship again, with the green road splitting around them.

SPOILER CEILING: no final five-node extinction, no full network-dead map, no post-Break world, no mature Shard/Fleet imagery, no successful rescue cluster, no issue-ending realization that the Cooperative Network is gone.
MUST AVOID: space battle, debris storm, wormhole cliché, lightning vortex, many ships in distress, giant explosion, abstract kaleidoscope, or effect density that makes the duplicated hull unreadable.

title: Issue 5 Cover — Three Ways to Survive
summary: Sell Issue 5 as politics being born through work. One battered piece of shared post-Break infrastructure is kept usable by three different survival habits: Ruben's improvised repair, Ava's person-to-person verified routing, and Iskara's accountable inspection. The common ancestral safety mark is central before anyone agrees what it will ultimately mean.
panelPlan: SINGLE FULL-BLEED PORTRAIT COVER centered on one battered but essential shared infrastructure element — a service junction/threshold whose continued operation visibly matters to ordinary people beyond the frame.
CAMERA: human-scale medium-wide, slightly low enough to make the repaired structure substantial but not heroic. The viewer should feel physically present at the worksite.

CENTERPIECE: the ancestral safety mark occupies the geometric center or near-center on the shared structure. It must read as one common practical mark, not three faction emblems and not a decorative logo floating over the scene.

RUBEN'S LOGIC: one side of the structure is physically kept alive by improvised bracework, salvage metal, clamps, rerouted conduit and practical field repair. Show hands/tools/material doing the argument.

AVA'S LOGIC: route assurance appears through tangible hand-verified objects — route tokens, tagged cargo/witness material, a physical route board or thread/map geometry — clearly indicating trusted movement without readable environmental text.

ISKARA'S LOGIC: inspection/accountability appears as a deliberate checked joint, seal, verification mark or inspection action tied directly to the safety symbol. Someone is willing to answer for what the mark promises.
Ruben, Ava and Iskara may all be visible, but none gets a poster stance. Their bodies should be absorbed in different kinds of work around the same shared problem.
ORDINARY HUMAN STAKES: include one or two background users/workers passing through or relying on the repaired threshold so the cover does not become an abstract doctrine diagram.
SHAPE LANGUAGE: one common center with three distinct practical vectors converging on it. The image must read as cooperation under tension, not a triptych.

PALETTE: rougher and more heterogeneous than Issues 1–4 — salvaged metals, warm work lights, residual greens, neutral cloth/materials. Foreshadow later traditions subtly through material behavior, not mature faction color blocking.
LIGHTING: patchwork practical illumination from work lamps, remaining civic fixtures and open environment. Preserve strong focal separation around the safety mark.
MASTHEAD ZONE: keep the upper field simpler than the work zone; weathered architecture can carry the title but no busy tool/hand action should sit directly behind it.
THUMBNAIL READ: one shared mark on one damaged structure, with three visibly different kinds of work keeping it useful.
SPOILER CEILING: no mature Core/Fleet/Verge/Shard faction branding, no resolved political settlement, no rescue-vessel reveal, no final doctrine codification, no triumphant unity image.

MUST AVOID: faction lineup, three equal portrait heads, propaganda-poster symmetry, mature blue/gold/white-vs-green-vs-red color teams, ruined-city despair, or abstract political iconography detached from physical survival.

title: Issue 6 Cover — Future on the Gantry
summary: Sell the finale as a future being assembled before its meaning is settled. A nearly ready prototype rescue vessel dominates the gantry, fed by mixed post-Break practices and carrying the shared ancestral safety mark. The ship looks consequential and capable but emphatically pre-Fleet; the unresolved command position is the quiet visual question.
panelPlan: SINGLE FULL-BLEED PORTRAIT FINALE COVER. The prototype rescue vessel is the hero object, occupying roughly 55–65% of the visual mass. It should dominate without becoming a glossy isolated ship beauty shot.

CAMERA: three-quarter gantry view from slightly below service-deck height, close enough to read the vessel's improvised construction and surrounding work, wide enough to show the rotunda/gantry ecosystem feeding into it.

SHIP DESIGN: practical, patched, multi-origin, robust, visibly assembled from post-Break constraints. It may contain ancestral hints of future Fleet design logic, but it must not look like a finished Rex Fleet vessel, military cruiser, or polished standardized class.
SHARED SAFETY MARK: place the ancestral mark prominently on a functional hull/service location. It should look applied for practical trust/accountability, not as a finished political logo.

CONVERGENCE OF PRACTICES: engineering salvage/brace hardware, hand-verified route material, annotated operating standards, relief supplies and mixed crew activity all physically feed toward the same vessel. Avoid separate faction staging zones.

UNRESOLVED COMMAND QUESTION: make one central command/captain position conspicuously unoccupied or visibly awaiting assignment through staging — an empty command chair seen through an open bridge aperture, an empty central boarding position, or a gap in an otherwise active preflight composition. Do not use readable roster text.

Iskara, Ruben and Ava may appear as small working figures in distinct operational roles. Their job is to show different practices converging; they must not stand shoulder-to-shoulder in front of the ship.
Liora is not physically present at the gantry and must not be inserted symbolically. Do not solve the absence by using a portrait/hologram of her.
ORDINARY STAKES: relief cargo, rescue equipment and civilian support activity should make clear that this is a service/rescue vessel, not the beginning of a war fleet.
SHAPE LANGUAGE: strong forward ship silhouette with gantry/work lines converging into it, while the empty command point creates a small counter-void inside an otherwise busy preparation image.

PALETTE: more open and hopeful than Issue 5 — mixed practical materials warmed by launch/work light, retained corridor green where appropriate, emerging blue/gold/white ancestry only as subtle material echoes rather than mature Fleet branding.
LIGHTING: dawn/launch-preparation feeling without triumphalist sunrise cliché. Use practical gantry sources and open-space light to make the vessel feel ready but unfinished.

MASTHEAD ZONE: maintain the approved founding trade-dress geometry exactly at its proper scope. Keep the vessel silhouette from colliding with the title; let structural lines lead toward, not through, the masthead.
THUMBNAIL READ: one compelling prototype ship almost ready to go; second read reveals the work of many systems feeding it and the conspicuously unresolved command place.
SPOILER CEILING: no vessel already launched, no escort formation, no mature Fleet uniforms/ships, no resolved captain assignment, no settled future faction order, no final historical interpretation.

MUST AVOID: generic cool-spaceship cover, mature Rex Fleet design pasted backward, military launch spectacle, heroic ensemble lineup, pristine standardized construction, or any image implying the politics are already solved.

settingText: Repurposed Cooperative logistics rotunda / Resolve Circle opening directly onto a service gantry where the prototype multiworld rescue vessel is being completed. Salvaged systems, relief cargo, hand-verified route material, inspection standards and mixed crews converge in one active launch-preparation environment.
